transcript:
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
The Supreme Court is allowing the Trump administration to resume, for now, deportations of migrants
to countries other than their birthplaces.
The Court is to hear oral arguments on the case in December, as NPR's Sergio Martinez-Beltron
reports.
The justices' brief order state a lower court order that blocked the third country deportations.
The court's three liberal justices objected.
The administration has said that a country's assurance that it will not engage in persecution
or torture should be enough to deport a non-citizen to a country that's not their own.
Solicitor General John Sauer told the justices third country deportations is "an essential
tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens."
The policy has been used to deport tens of thousands of non-citizens to countries in
Africa and Latin America, where their attorneys say the migrants face significant harms.
Sergio Martinez-Beltron, NPR News, Austin, Texas.
Hurricane Polo's remnants are bringing more rain to the flood-struck Southwest.
Flood watches extend from Arizona into Central Texas.
In New Mexico, state officials report flooded roads and debris on highways.
There have been several water rescues in Arizona.
President Trump has released what the White House says is a voluntary accord with major
tech companies on artificial intelligence, saying they've agreed to self-police AI development.
They love our country, they love the world, and they came together and they did something
that few people really, it's almost like a constitution in a way.
And the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it
really is a form of protection.
Trump unveiled a one-page document on social media after meeting with tech executives for
a Tuesday lunch at the White House.
Trump says AI companies are capable of self-policing.
The agreement comes amid alarm bells sounded by AI executives who've called on the government
to establish guardrails.
After more than two tumultuous decades, the U.S. military formally pulls out of Iraq Wednesday.
The withdrawal will also mark the end of the anti-ISIS coalition that the U.S. has led
since 2014, as NPR's Jane Arras reports from Baghdad.
At what had been the Joint Military Command Center, Iraqi workers are renovating.
U.S. officers have operated from here since 2014, when Iraq asked the U.S. military to
return to fight the militant group ISIS.
On Wednesday, U.S. commanders and Iraqi leaders will mark the withdrawal of U.S. forces 23
years after the United States invaded Iraq.
It's a historical day.
We are very proud to reach this day.
That's Iraqi Armed Forces spokesman Sabah al-Nouman.
At its height during an eight-year-long occupation, the U.S. had 170,000 military personnel in
Iraq.
Jane Arras and Pure News begged Dad.
And you're listening to NPR News from Washington.
The union representing 8,000 EPA employees nationwide has filed a lawsuit over the agency's
termination of their union contract last year from Member Station GBH, Craig LaMoltezmore.
The EPA terminated its union contract last summer after President Trump signed an executive
order ending collective bargaining rights for more than a million federal employees.
Lilly Simmons heads AFGE Local 3428, which represents EPA employees in New England.
She says those workers have lost protections that were in the contract.
For example, you go out and you do some water sampling, and it's bad.
And you need to share that bad news, and you need to make sure that people are not using
that water as a source of drinking water.
But are you going to lose your job for saying so?
That is a real concern for people.
The executive order cited national security concerns.
The EPA has not responded to a request for comment.
For NPR News, I'm Craig LaMoltez in Boston.
In English Premier League soccer, Manchester City is facing repercussions after an independent
commission found City guilty of almost all of the 115 charges of financial wrongdoing.
The league's chief executive, Richard Masters, says the commission's verdict details how
the club systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade.
The club denies wrongdoing and says in a statement that it will appeal.
Alaska's Fat Bear Contest has a winner, a brown bear named Backpack, as this year's
champion voted the winner of Fat Bear Week at Alaska's Katmai National Park and Preserve.
He's estimated to weigh more than 1,000 pounds.
I'm Charles Snyder.
This is NPR News.

Hurricane Polo remnants bring more rain to flood-struck Southwest, extending from Arizona to Texas
President Trump releases voluntary AI accord with major tech companies on self-policing development
U.S. military formally withdraws from Iraq after more than two decades of involvement
EPA union representing 8,000 employees nationwide files lawsuit over terminated union contract
Manchester City found guilty of almost all 115 charges of financial wrongdoing by independent commission
Backpack, brown bear, wins Alaska's Fat Bear Week contest, weighing over 1,000 pounds
